title: Linked List
tagline: Pointer surgery without an array — dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and the in-place reversal that solves half the questions.
intro:
A linked list stores elements in **nodes**, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array, the nodes aren't contiguous in memory — you can only reach a node by following pointers from the head. That gives O(1) insertion/deletion once you hold the right node, but O(n) access by position (no indexing).

Linked-list interview questions are really **pointer-manipulation** puzzles. The difficulty is never the algorithm — it's not losing your place: reconnecting pointers in the right order, handling the head specially, and avoiding null dereferences. Three techniques defuse almost all of it: the **dummy head** sentinel (kills head edge-cases), **fast/slow pointers** (find middle, detect cycles, nth-from-end), and **in-place reversal** (the single most-tested operation).

This module gives you all three with safe templates and the order-of-operations that prevents the classic 'lost the rest of the list' bug.
objectives: Manipulate next pointers without losing the remainder of the list
Use a dummy head to eliminate special-casing the first node
Reverse a linked list in place, iteratively and recursively
Apply fast/slow pointers for middle, cycle detection, and nth-from-end
Merge two sorted lists and detect/remove cycles
Reason about why linked-list ops are O(1) given the node, O(n) to find it

signals: Frequent insertions/deletions at known positions, no random access needed
"Reverse the list / reverse in groups of k"
"Find the middle", "nth node from the end", "detect a cycle"
The head node itself might be removed/changed → use a dummy
antiSignals: You need index access or binary search → array
You need to sort by value repeatedly → array or heap

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
A linked list is a treasure hunt. Each clue (a node) holds a prize (a value) and tells you where the next clue is hidden. You can't leap straight to clue number five - you have to follow the trail from the very first clue. That is why there is no instant jump-to-index like an array gives you.

Example (reversing a list): to turn the trail around, flip each arrow to point backward, one at a time. The trick is to jot down where you were about to go *before* you flip the arrow, so you don't lose the rest of the trail. Three little pointers - previous, current, and the saved next - shuffle forward together until the whole list points the other way.

sections.heading: Node anatomy and core trade-offs
sections.body:
| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Node** | `{ val, next }` — a value plus a pointer to the next node |
| **Head** | First node; `null`/`None` head means empty list |
| **Singly linked** | Each node points only forward (`next`) |
| **Doubly linked** | Nodes also point back (`prev`) — O(1) delete given the node |
| **Dummy / sentinel** | A fake node before the head to simplify edge-cases |

The defining trade-off versus an array:

| Operation | Array | Linked list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access by index | O(1) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at known node | O(n) (shift) | O(1) (relink) |
| Search by value | O(n) | O(n) |

sections.heading: The dummy-head technique
sections.body:
Half of linked-list bugs come from the head being a special case (removing the first node, building a new list). A **dummy head** — a throwaway node placed before the real head — erases that special case: you always have a node *before* the one you're working on, so insertion and deletion are uniform. At the end, return `dummy.next`.

Reach for a dummy whenever the head might change: removing nodes, merging lists, partitioning.

sections.heading: In-place reversal (the most-tested op)
sections.body:
Reversing a singly linked list is the operation behind reverse-list, reverse-in-k-groups, palindrome-check, and reorder-list. The iterative version walks the list once, flipping each `next` pointer to point backward, using three pointers: `prev`, `curr`, and a saved `next`.

The critical order of operations: **save `next` before you overwrite `curr.next`**, or you lose the rest of the list. Memorise the four-line dance.

codeExamples.label: Reverse a linked list (iterative)
codeExamples.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next     # 1. save the rest
        curr.next = prev    # 2. flip the pointer
        prev = curr         # 3. advance prev
        curr = nxt          # 4. advance curr
    return prev             # new head

codeExamples.label: Reverse a linked list (iterative)

callouts.text: The #1 linked-list bug: overwriting `curr.next` before saving it. Always capture `nxt = curr.next` on the first line of the loop body.

sections.heading: Fast/slow pointers on lists
sections.body:
Two pointers from the head, `fast` moving twice as fast as `slow`, solve a cluster of problems in one pass with O(1) space:

| Task | How |
| --- | --- |
| Find the middle | When `fast` hits the end, `slow` is at the middle |
| Detect a cycle | If `fast` ever equals `slow`, there's a loop (Floyd's) |
| Find cycle start | After meeting, reset one pointer to head; advance both 1× until they meet |
| Nth node from end | Advance `fast` n steps first, then move both until `fast` ends |

This beats the naive 'store visited nodes in a hash set' approach on space — O(1) vs O(n).

sections.heading: Merging two sorted lists
sections.body: Merging is the linked-list half of merge sort and a frequent standalone question. Use a dummy head and a `tail` pointer; repeatedly attach the smaller of the two front nodes and advance that list. When one list empties, attach the remainder of the other in O(1).

interviewTalking: Draw the list and the pointers on the whiteboard first — interviewers expect it and it prevents lost-pointer bugs. Say: "I'll use a dummy head so I don't special-case the original head, and I'll save the next pointer before relinking so I never lose the tail." For middle/cycle problems, name fast/slow: "Two pointers, fast moving twice as fast — O(1) space instead of a hash set of visited nodes." State O(n) time, O(1) space.
commonMistakes: Overwriting `curr.next` before saving it — loses the rest of the list
Not using a dummy head, then writing fragile special-cases for the first node
Returning `head` instead of `dummy.next` after the head may have changed
Creating a cycle by mis-ordering pointer assignments
Using O(n) extra space (hash set) for cycle detection when fast/slow is O(1)
complexityNotes: Most linked-list algorithms are a single pass: O(n) time, O(1) space. Recursive reversal is O(n) time but O(n) stack space. Access by position is O(n); insertion/deletion is O(1) once you hold the predecessor node.
